record.field: A concurrent update fails the first attempts with 40001; a retry succeeds.

field.name: description
field.p: Another user updates the row and commits while this request waits for the row lock. Under REPEATABLE READ a transaction may not overwrite a row that changed after its snapshot, so PostgreSQL raises 40001 could not serialize access due to concurrent update. retrying() rolls back, sleeps a random time and runs the whole call again; the next attempt has a fresh snapshot and succeeds.
Look at: the first attempts rolled back with SERIALIZATION_FAILURE, each with a backoff below 2 s, then 4 s; the last attempt committed. The row gains 100 from you and 1 from each competing update.

record.field: Two flows lock rows A and B in opposite orders: 40P01.

field.name: description
field.p: This request locks row A then row B; a background flow locks B then A. Each waits for the other. After deadlock_timeout (1 s by default) PostgreSQL aborts one of them with 40P01 deadlock detected. The request started waiting first, so its deadlock check runs first and it is the victim; retrying() runs it again.
Look at: attempt 1 rolled back with DEADLOCK_DETECTED after about deadlock_timeout, attempt 2 committed. The fix is to lock rows in the same order in every code path.

record.field: FOR UPDATE NOWAIT against a held lock: 55P03, retried until the lock is gone.

field.name: description
field.p: Another transaction holds a lock on the row for a few seconds. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT fails at once with 55P03 could not obtain lock on row instead of waiting, and retrying() tries again with a growing random backoff until the lock is released. Odoo 19 uses NOWAIT on purpose in no-gap sequences, loyalty codes, POS session opening and Studio approvals.
Look at: rolled-back attempts with LOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE, then a commit. With an unlucky draw of short backoffs the five attempts can all fall inside the lock: that is the exhaustion case.
ORM lock_for_update(): the 19.0 helper locks with SKIP LOCKED and raises LockError, a UserError: one attempt, no retry, the user gets "Cannot grab a lock on records".

record.field: A row stays hot longer than all five attempts: the error reaches the user.

field.name: description
field.p: A background writer updates and commits the row many times a second for up to 45 s. Each attempt reads the row, works for 0.3 s and writes it back: 40001 every time. After the fifth failure retrying() logs maximum number of tries reached! and the error reaches the user.

Look at: five rolled-back attempts, four backoffs bounded by 2, 4, 8 and 16 s, no backoff after the fifth. Expect about 15 s of waiting on average, about 30 s at worst, plus the time of the attempts themselves.

record.field: An IntegrityError becomes a ValidationError at the first attempt, never retried.

field.name: description
field.p: Two users create a row with the same unique code at the same moment. Our check finds nothing (the other row is not in our snapshot), our INSERT waits for the other transaction and then fails with 23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint. That is an IntegrityError: retrying() rolls back and raises a ValidationError with the constraint message at once. It never retries it, even though a retry would have found the row.

Get or create, ConcurrencyError: the code catches the violation and raises odoo.exceptions.ConcurrencyError, new in 19.0 and retried like 40001: attempt 2 finds the row and updates it. Enterprise account_invoice_extract does the same for partners created by OCR.

record.field: An external call made inside the transaction runs once per attempt.

field.name: description
field.p: Confirming the order sends the confirmation (an email, an API call) straight away, inside the transaction. The ORM writes the order at the flush, which retrying() runs after the method returned: the UPDATE meets a concurrent edit and fails with 40001. Every attempt had already sent its message, and nothing takes it back.
Look at: one confirmed order, one external call per attempt in Outside world.

Confirm order, cr.commit() midway: the code commits after confirming the order, then a later write meets the conflict. retrying() can only roll back what came after the commit, so each retry confirms the order again: its value grows by one per attempt.

record.field: The same flow with cr.postcommit or an outbox: one external call per click.

field.name: description
field.p: Confirm order (postcommit): the call is registered with self.env.cr.postcommit.add(...). The rollback of a failed attempt clears the queue, so the call runs once, after the commit. If it fails then, the order stays confirmed: nothing retries the call.

Confirm order (outbox): the message is a row written in the same transaction; a failed attempt rolls it back with the order. Deliver outbox plays the worker: it sends each pending message with its idempotency key, at least once. Tick Crash after delivery, deliver, untick, deliver again: the receiver gets the message twice and ignores the second copy.

record.field: Eight simultaneous increments: where updates get lost, and where they only retry.

field.name: description
field.p: Each button sends simultaneous requests that add 1 to the same counter, each in its own thread and cursor and through the real retrying(), as an RPC call would.

ul.li: Read-modify-write and SET value = value + 1: under REPEATABLE READ neither loses an update inside one transaction. Both conflict with 40001 and retry; the atomic UPDATE only has a smaller conflict window.

Stale form value: the value was read in an earlier transaction, like a form loaded before the save. The saves do not overlap, so there is no error and no retry, and the counter ends well below the number of requests.
Insert-only ledger: one row per increment, nothing to conflict on.

field.p: Look at: the note expected +8, got +N and the retries of each run.

record.field: The 40001 of the first scenario, in a scheduled action: no retry.

field.name: description
field.p: The job hits the conflict of the first scenario. ir.cron does not call retrying(): the job fails at once, the error is logged, the failure count goes up and the job waits for its next call.

ul.li: Run Manually: in 19.0 the button runs the job like the scheduler does, on its own cursor, so there is no retry either (17.0 ran it inside the HTTP request, which retried it).
Trigger the cron worker: the real scheduler path. It needs a cron thread (max_cron_threads > 0) working on this database.
Batched job: the job commits its progress after each row with _commit_progress(). When it fails after committing some progress, ir.cron runs it again at once, without backoff, and it ends fully done.
Pretend a week of failures: the next failure deactivates the job (19.0: 5 consecutive failures spanning more than 7 days).

record.field: retrying() rewinds uploaded files before it retries, or raises RuntimeError.

field.name: description
field.p: A controller reads an uploaded file, then hits a serialization failure. Before the retry, retrying() rewinds each file of request.httprequest.files, or raises RuntimeError: Cannot retry request on input file ... after serialization failure when the stream cannot seek.
The check runs before the error is classified: with a unique violation (never retried) the user still gets the RuntimeError instead of the validation message.
